sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do the main image and the headline make one idea together, with neither just repeating the other?** No.
   - **Where:** The headline at y≈145 says "Savings deposits rose every month". The chart (x 48–848, y 218–693) agrees for January to May, but its most striking mark is June at $1150k. That bar jumps about $282k (about 32%) over May, while each earlier month rose by only $40k to $80k.
   - **What the viewer meets:** The headline doesn't explain that jump, and neither does the subtitle at y≈185. The reason sits only in the small grey source line at y≈717: "June includes the mid-year bonus payroll." The headline and the chart read as one unbroken growth story. Most members won't read the source line, so they'll take June as normal growth. The $4.82M total and the "Up 6.1%" card at x 880–1232 are inflated by a one-off, which the page never states.
   - **Why:** The catalog entry for this line has no approved source, so this is common sense. A headline should name what the picture makes the viewer ask about. On a report people trust for numbers, it shouldn't let the picture make a claim the footnote takes back.
   - **Fix:** Make the headline and chart tell the same story, June included. Either the headline names it ("Deposits rose every month, with a one-off jump in June from the bonus payroll"), or the chart marks June's bonus share directly, as a split or annotated bar. Then the caveat sits where the eye already goes.
   - **Type and weight:** Defect, major.
2. **Does every element, rule, box, and ornament do a job, so that removing it would lose something?** No.
   - **Where:** The chart card title at y≈250, "Deposits into savings accounts, US dollars per month", repeats the subtitle directly above it at y≈185, "New money paid into member savings accounts, by month, January to June 2026."
   - **What the viewer meets:** They read the same statement twice, about 65 px apart, in two different voices. The only new information is the unit "US dollars", and the axis labels already show that.
   - **Why:** Common sense. Nielsen's aesthetic and minimalist design heuristic (no. 8) also says extra information competes with the information that matters.
   - **Fix:** Keep one. Either drop the chart title or cut it to the unit. Better still, use that slot for the June note from finding 1.
   - **Type and weight:** Convention, minor.

   The diagonal hatching on a single-series bar chart also does no job and makes the bars shimmer. That belongs under Charts and data, so I left it to that critic.

**What's working.**
- The page has one consistent quiet system: a navy serif for the headline and wordmark, a neutral sans for everything else, one blue for the data and green only for "Up" deltas. It reads as one sober institution, which suits a credit union reporting members' money.
- Each heading and card label says exactly what its number is, including the time period: "Total deposited, Jan to Jun 2026", "Average deposit, Jun 2026", "Accounts that made a deposit, Jun 2026". Nobody has to guess what $214 or 5,374 means.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 6 yes, 2 no (main image and headline make one idea; every element does a job), 0 unsure.

sections.report:
**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Below the first element, can you tell each level of the text (title, headings, body, captions) from the next at a glance, with no two sizes almost the same?** No.
   - **Where:** The headline "Savings deposits rose every month" (heavy serif, about 30 px, x 48–590, y 128–162) is about the same size as the three KPI figures in the right column ($4.82M at y ~262–295, $214 at ~402–432, 5,374 at ~541–572). Those figures are bold sans, about 32 px, so they look as large as the headline or slightly larger.
   - **What the viewer experiences:** The headline still wins on position and length, so the eye starts in the right place. But the next level down isn't clear. Three same-size numbers pull the eye right before it has read the subtitle or the chart, so the page has two co-equal tops: the claim and a stack of totals.
   - **Second problem:** Below that, the small text forms a cluster of sizes only a pixel or two apart: subtitle ~16 px, nav and chart title ~15, KPI labels and deltas ~14, eyebrow and source ~13, axis labels ~12. Weight, caps and colour separate most of these, which is the right tool. The one clash is the subtitle (y ~185) and the KPI labels ("Total deposited, Jan to Jun 2026" and the rest). Both are regular grey sans, close in size, but they do different jobs.
   - **Why:** A hierarchy needs two to four levels you can tell apart at a glance (Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems in Graphic Design*). Sizes should come from a small set of distinct steps (Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*, 3.1.1). Small differences leave the eye unsure whether two things are equal or unequal (Dair, *Design with Type*, ch. 8; Arnheim).
   - **Fix:** Put the headline and the KPI figures on clearly different steps of the scale. Either drop the KPI figures to about 24 px so they read as supporting evidence under the claim, or enlarge the headline to about 40 px. Collapse the 12–16 px cluster to two sizes, and use weight and colour for any finer distinctions.
   - Convention. Weight: minor, because the first read still lands on the headline.

**What's working.**
- **Headline style and wording:** The headline has its own form: a heavy serif that matches the wordmark, against sans everywhere else. It is also the only full sentence at display size. That makes it the clear entry point, and it states the finding instead of labelling the topic.
- **Headings differ by more than size:** Every level differs from its neighbours by more than size. The eyebrow is tracked caps, the chart title is bold, and the KPI labels are grey with dark figures beneath. Even where sizes sit close, the roles stay readable.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 2 yes, 1 no (text levels distinct, no two sizes almost the same)

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Do lines of text in neighboring columns sit on the same baselines?** No. Where the two columns start, the chart title "Deposits into savings accounts, US dollars per month" has its baseline at about y≈255. Across the 32 px gutter, the first KPI label "Total deposited, Jan to Jun 2026" sits at about y≈251. Both panels start at y≈218 and have the same 20 px padding, so the two first lines look like they're meant to share a line but miss by about 4 px. The miss is small, but it's right where the eye crosses from the chart to the KPIs, and it makes the two columns look like they were built separately. Müller-Brockmann (*Grid Systems in Graphic Design*, "Construction of the grid") says lines in neighboring fields share baselines. Fix: match the chart title's line box to the KPI label's (same line height and top padding) so the two first lines sit level. **Convention**, minor.
2. **Is the empty space gathered into a few deliberate areas, rather than left over in scattered small gaps?** No. Under the KPI stack there's an empty patch about 350×180 px (x 880–1232, y 619–800). It's there because the three cards end about 75 px above the chart panel's bottom (y≈694), not because the space was planned. It reads like a missing fourth card, and the bottom of the page looks unfinished rather than calm. Ruder and Tschichold both say empty space should be shaped on purpose, and that a large unexplained empty area is a fault. Fix: make the two columns end together, either by spacing or sizing the three cards so the last one ends at y≈694, or by putting something real in that area (for example the source/June note, which applies to the KPIs too). If the stack must stay short, let the space look intended rather than like a gap. **Taste**, minor.

**What's working.**
- The grid is strict and consistent. There are 48 px outer margins on both sides, an 800 / 32 / 352 column split (about two-thirds to one-third of the content width), 16 px between cards, and 20 px inner padding in every panel. Text inside the panels starts at the same inset everywhere, so the page feels built rather than assembled.
- The reading order is clear without help. The eye goes kicker → headline → deck → chart (the main evidence, in the wide left column) → KPI cards on the right. The top edges of the chart and KPI panels align at y≈218, so it's obvious that both columns start together.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 11 yes, 2 no (lines in neighboring columns share baselines; empty space is gathered, not left over)

**Section.** Text: applies. The text is short: a wordmark, nav, eyebrow, headline, subhead, chart title and labels, three stat cards, and a source line.

**Findings**

None. Every line in the Text checklist is yes.

The two notes below are about the wording. The checklist has no line for either, so the director should rank them or pass them on:

1. **Wording, no checklist line: "Up 6.1% on Jan to Jun 2025", "Up $11 on Jun 2025" and "Up 402 on Jun 2025"** (the green lines at about x 900, y 313, 452 and 591). "Up X on <period>" is newsroom shorthand for "compared with". A member can read it as "went up on that date", or have to stop and work out which period is being compared. These are the figures a member will remember and repeat, so a second reading matters. The fix is to name the comparison: "Up 6.1% on the same months of 2025", or "vs Jun 2025". Defect, minor. This is common sense; no source in the catalog covers it.
2. **Wording, no checklist line: "Average deposit, Jun 2026 / $214"** (card 2, about x 900, y 385). It doesn't say what is averaged: each deposit transaction, or each account that made a deposit. 5,374 accounts and roughly $1.15M in June works out to about $214 per account, so it is probably per account. A member reading "average deposit" will more likely take it as per transaction. The fix is to make the label say which, for example "Average deposited per account, Jun 2026". Defect, minor. This is also common sense with no catalog source.
   - A smaller related point: the bar labels "$1150k" (x 752, y 297) have no thousands separator and use a different unit from the "$4.82M" card next to them, while "5,374" does have a comma. That belongs to the Data or Interface critic, not Text, so I'm only flagging it here.

**What's working.**
- **The type plan is clear.** One serif carries the wordmark and the headline. One sans carries everything else, with only weight and grey separating the levels (chart title, label, figure, delta). The page reads as one system with no near-matching faces.
- **The headline makes a claim.** "Savings deposits rose every month" gives a finding instead of a topic, and the subhead says what is measured and over which months. A member knows the point before reading the chart.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 30 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

Walk (working notes), Color section:
- Small palette: yes (navy wordmark, neutral grays, one chart blue, one green for status)
- Saturated color kept to a small share: yes
- Clear range of light and dark: yes
- Warm forward, cool recedes: yes (all cool, and nothing needs to come forward through warmth)
- Matching colors look the same everywhere: yes
- No vibrating edges between strong colors: yes (no strong neighbours outside the chart, and the chart's striped fill belongs to the data section)
- Status colors used only for their usual meaning: yes (green = increase)
- Color meaning also given another way: yes ("Up" is written out)
- Dark theme background: yes (not a dark theme)

No line was answered no or unsure, so I opened no entries.

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **Disciplined palette.** The page uses one neutral gray range, a dark navy for the wordmark and the active nav item, one mid blue for the chart, and one green kept for the "Up …" change lines in the three cards on the right (x ≈ 900–1090, y ≈ 312, 451, 590). Strong color covers only a small part of the page: the bars and three short lines of green. So the blue bars are clearly where the eye should go, and nothing else competes with them. Keep the blue for the data alone.
- **Green means good, and the words say it too.** The green is used only for increases, which is the usual meaning for members reading about their money. Each green line also starts with the word "Up", so a reader who can't see the green, or sees the page in grayscale, gets the same message.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure.

**Walk (working notes).** The image is 1280×800, one screen, so no crops were needed. The only pictorial element is the "Brookhollow Credit Union" wordmark at the top left (about x 48–332, y 18–44). There are no photos, illustrations or icons. The hatched bars belong to the chart, so the checklist routes them to "Charts and data".
- Image shows its content: yes
- Full quality: yes, the wordmark looks crisp
- Crop intended: yes, nothing is cropped
- Figure-ground: yes
- One rendering style: yes
- Photos consistent: yes, there are none
- Icon strokes consistent: yes, there are none
- One viewpoint and light: yes, there is no scene
- Texture quiet: yes for pictures. The diagonal hatching in the bars is a chart fill and goes to the data section.
- No fake depth: yes
- Logo clear space, undistorted, own colours: yes
- Logo simple enough to read small and in one colour: yes

No line is `no` or `unsure`, so there are no entries to open.

---

**Section.** Pictures: applies, but only to the "Brookhollow Credit Union" wordmark. The page has no photos, illustrations or icons.

**Findings**
None.

Note for the director: the dense diagonal hatching in all six bars (about x 160–785, y 310–638) is the only texture on the page. It's a chart fill, so the checklist files it under "Charts and data", not here. To my eye it shimmers at this stripe spacing and competes with the value labels above the bars. The data critic should judge whether a solid fill would serve better.

**What's working.** The wordmark is a plain navy serif setting with generous space around it in the header bar (about 48 px to the left edge and 40 px to the first nav item). It reads instantly at this size, it would survive in one colour, and its serif matches the page headline, which ties the brand to the report.

**Checklist.** Pictures: 12 lines, 12 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Section.** Charts and data: applies. There is one monthly bar chart and three KPI cards with comparisons.

**Findings**
1. **Is nearly all the ink in each chart data, with no 3D, shadows, textures, or heavy gridlines?** No. All six bars (x about 163–783, y 312–637) are filled with dense blue-and-white diagonal stripes. On screen these vibrate, and the eye goes to the texture before the bar heights or the value labels. The stripes encode nothing: every bar has the same pattern. Patterned fills are chartjunk that competes with the data (Few, "Common Pitfalls in Dashboard Design", pitfall 11; Tufte, *Visual Display*, ch. 5). Fix: draw the bars in a plain flat blue. If a mark is needed for the one-off in June (see finding 2), use the pattern or a lighter tint on the June bar only, so the texture carries meaning. Defect (convention, sourced). Weight: major, because the chart is the centrepiece and the stripes are the loudest thing in it.
2. **Does a title or caption state the chart's finding in words?** No, in part. The headline "Savings deposits rose every month" states the trend. But the most striking mark, June's jump from $868k to $1150k (+$282k, against +$43k to +$79k in each earlier month), is explained only in the grey source line under the card ("June includes the mid-year bonus payroll", y about 717). That line is the smallest, palest text on the page and sits outside the chart. Members will read the June bar as growth speeding up, not as a one-off. The headline's "rose every month" and the "$4.82M, up 6.1%" card both lean on that bar without saying so. The catalog's source for this entry is off the approved list, so this is common sense: when the biggest feature of a chart has a cause the viewer needs to know, the note belongs at the mark. Fix: put a short note next to the June bar ("Includes mid-year bonus payroll"). If the bonus can be split out, show June without it as well, so members can see the underlying trend. Defect. Weight: major, because it changes what members take away about their credit union's growth.

**What's working.**
- The bars run from a $0k baseline with even $300k ticks, and every bar has its exact value above it. Bar lengths are honest and members don't need to read values off the axis.
- Each KPI card puts a unit, a period and a year-on-year change under its big number ("Up 6.1% on Jan to Jun 2025", "Up 402 on Jun 2025"), so none of the figures stands alone (Few, pitfall 2).

**Checklist.** Charts and data: 16 lines, 14 yes, 2 no (nearly all ink is data, no textures; title or caption states the finding)

Walk (Interface). The only controls are the top navigation: the "Brookhollow Credit Union" wordmark and four links (Accounts, Member report, Rates, Branches). There are no buttons, fields, dialogs or errors. The image is 1280×800, so no crops are needed.

- One primary action: yes. This is a report page with no actions to rank.
- Controls look like what they do: yes. Nav links sit in a standard top bar.
- 3:1 for control edges and icons: yes. There are none.
- Hover, pressed and disabled states distinct: yes. None are shown.
- Focus indicator 2 px at 3:1: unsure. A still can't show it.
- Focus not obscured: unsure. A still can't show it, and the header doesn't appear to be sticky.
- Main content uncovered: yes.
- Target size: yes. The nav labels are about 17 px tall but sit roughly 28 px apart, so the WCAG 2.5.8 spacing exception covers them.
- Phone thumb zone: yes. This is a desktop layout.
- Shows where the user is: yes. "Member report" is bold and navy, and the eyebrow says "MEMBER REPORT, FIRST HALF 2026".
- Way out: yes. There is no dialog.
- Valid inputs, destructive actions, recall, progressive disclosure, field labels, mapping, one-column form, required fields, error wording, error fix, empty states, help, shortcuts: yes. None of these are present or needed.
- Anticipation: yes. The figures the reader came for are on the first screen.
- Conventions: yes. Logo at left, nav beside it.
- Audience's words: yes. The nav labels are plain.
- Link purpose: yes.
- Sensory instructions: yes. There are none.
- Conceptual model: yes.
- Consistency across screens: yes. Only one screen is shown.
- Reflow at this width: yes.
- Dark patterns: yes. There are none.

No line ended at `no`, so I didn't open any reference entries. The two focus lines stay `unsure` because only a live page can answer them.

**Section.** Interface: applies, but only in a small way. The only controls are the top navigation (wordmark plus four links, y ≈ 15–45). There are no buttons, forms, dialogs or messages.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **The nav shows where you are.** "Member report" (x ≈ 467–577, y ≈ 30) is set in bold navy against the grey of the other links. The "MEMBER REPORT, FIRST HALF 2026" eyebrow at y ≈ 105 says the same thing. The reader can tell where they are in the site without hunting (Nielsen 1, visibility of system status). Keep both cues when revising.
- **The header follows the usual layout.** The wordmark sits at left with the links right beside it, and the bar is set off by a hairline rule. Members recognise it at once, so it takes no attention from the report below (Jakob's law).

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Hover and keyboard-focus states on the four nav links. The page offers nothing else to act on, so these links are the only way to move around. Check in a live browser that a focus ring shows on each one.
- Whether the header stays pinned when the page scrolls. If it does, check that it doesn't cover focused content.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 31 yes, 0 no, 2 unsure (focused control shows a 2 px indicator at 3:1; focused control not covered by sticky header). I couldn't judge either from a still.
